**Setup.** A knight move changes x and y by (±1, ±3) or (±3, ±1), so x+y changes by an even amount. Each path therefore stays within the squares of one colour (x+y even or x+y odd). The 13 even squares and 12 odd squares form separate graphs.

**Even squares.** The centre (2,2) has no moves. Among the other 12 even squares, four squares (1,1), (1,3), (3,1), (3,3) have degree 4, and the other eight have degree 2. Each degree-2 square is a subdivision of an edge between two degree-4 squares. A path can visit each degree-4 square at most once, and two degree-2 squares are never adjacent. So a path has at most 4 branch squares, at most 3 subdivision squares between them, and at most 2 more at the ends, giving at most 9 squares. A path of length 9 exists:
(2,4), (1,1), (4,2), (1,3), (0,0), (3,1), (0,2), (3,3), (2,0).

**Odd squares.** The 12 odd squares are (0,1), (0,3), (1,0), (1,2), (1,4), (2,1), (2,3), (3,0), (3,2), (3,4), (4,1), (4,3). A path through all 12 exists:

(3,2), (0,3), (1,0), (2,3), (3,0), (0,1), (1,4), (2,1), (3,4), (4,1), (1,2), (4,3).

Each consecutive pair differs by (±1, ±3) or (±3, ±1), and all 12 squares are distinct. Since the odd component has only 12 squares, this is optimal for that colour.

**Conclusion.** The longest possible path is on the odd squares, with 12 squares, which beats the 9 available on the even squares.
